prime.problem: Making a model better usually means training a bigger one, which is expensive. A smaller model could instead spend more compute on each question, but nobody knew when that pays off or how to spend it.
prime.fits: Builds on self-consistency (many samples, then a vote) and process reward models (a verifier that scores steps). This card asks how to spend a fixed answering budget, and when it beats a bigger model.
expect: best-of-N vs beam search against a PRM
prime.goal: Choose between search, revisions and a bigger model for a given question difficulty and usage level, and explain why test-time compute can't help on questions the model never solves.

attend: What can a verifier do with 16 samples when none of them is right?
Why would stronger search make easy questions worse rather than better?
What does revising in sequence do that sampling in parallel can't, and the other way round?
How is a question's difficulty estimated when the answer isn't known, and what does that cost?
Why does the number of questions you'll ask the model (R) change whether a bigger model is worth it?

must: Test-time compute can only select or refine answers the model can already produce → if the pass rate is near 0, more tries add nothing → on the hardest questions a bigger model is the only lever
Easy question → the first try is nearly right → local revisions fix it → all-sequential is best; harder question → it needs a different approach → parallel samples explore → a mix of both is best

Search optimises the verifier's score → pushed hard, it exploits the verifier's mistakes (filler steps, one- or two-step solutions) → beam search hurts easy questions at large budgets and helps medium ones

A bigger model costs more to train and on every answer → FLOPs matching gives the small model ≈258× its one-answer compute at R = 0.16 but only ≈16× at R = 22 → test-time compute wins with light usage and on easy questions, pretraining wins with heavy usage on hard ones
elevated: Revision models turn about 38% of right answers wrong → you still need a verifier or a vote to pick the final answer from the chain
Difficulty bins come from 2,048 samples per question → choosing per bin gives 2–4× efficiency, but that estimation cost isn't counted
reference: Setting: PaLM 2-S*, MATH 12k train / 500 test; models fine-tuned to revise and to verify
PRM trained from Monte Carlo rollouts, not human labels; final-step score; best-of-N weighted selection
Compute-optimal vs best-of-N: revisions 64 vs 256 generations (Fig. 8); search nearly matches 16 vs 64 (Fig. 4)
Fig. 1 revisions vs 14× model: R = 0.16 easy/medium/hard +21.6 / +27.8 / +11.8%; R = 22 +5.4 / −24.3 / −37.2%
FLOPs: pretraining 6·N·D, inference 2·N·D; allowed multiplier M + 3(M − 1)/R

compress.prompt: From memory, explain in 3–5 sentences when a small model with extra test-time compute beats a bigger model, and how to spend the extra compute. Or redraw the three-columns-by-three-rows sketch.
checklist: two ways to spend it: search against a verifier, or sequential revisions
easy questions favour revisions; harder ones favour a mix with parallel search
choosing per difficulty gives up to 4× efficiency over best-of-N
it beats a 14× model on easy/medium questions when inference use is light
on the hardest questions, or with heavy use, pretraining a bigger model wins

retrieve.q: Explain what 'compute-optimal' test-time scaling means and why it beats a fixed best-of-N.
answer: pick the method and settings per question, based on estimated difficulty
different difficulties favour different methods
a fixed strategy wastes compute where it's the wrong tool
up to 4× less compute for the same accuracy

retrieve.q: Walk through how a revision model plus a verifier answers one question with a budget of 16.
answer: the model writes a first attempt
each next attempt sees up to the four previous ones and tries to fix them
repeat to 16 attempts (or split into parallel chains)
the verifier picks the best answer within and across chains, because revisions can break right answers

retrieve.q: Your model will serve millions of hard competition questions. Do you spend extra compute at test time or on a bigger model? Justify it with the paper.
answer: heavy usage means large R, so FLOPs matching leaves little spare test-time compute
hard questions gain little from more tries
Fig. 1: hard questions at R = 22 are −37.2% (revisions) and −52.9% (search)
a bigger model is the better spend

compare.q: Majority voting and best-of-N with a verifier both spend compute on parallel samples. What does the verifier add, and why does the paper's search sometimes do worse than plain sampling?
answer: voting needs no extra model; it picks the most common answer
a verifier can pick a right minority answer
but a verifier can be exploited by stronger search
at high budgets beam search fell below best-of-N

compare.q: This paper spends extra compute with external machinery (a verifier, a revision loop). s1 makes one model think longer in a single chain. What's fundamentally different, and what does each need?
answer: here: separate verifier and revision fine-tuning, many generations
s1: one long chain of thought, extended by forcing 'Wait'
s1 needs no verifier but relies on the model checking itself
both still can't produce what the model doesn't know

compare.q: From a user's point of view, what does test-time compute cost that the FLOPs comparison ignores?
answer: latency: sequential revisions can't run in parallel
more output tokens per answer
parallel samples cost throughput but not much wall time

predict.q: Suppose someone builds a perfect verifier that never makes mistakes. Which of the paper's findings would change, and which would stay?
predict.answer: Search would stop degrading at large budgets on easy questions, because there would be no verifier errors to exploit. Best-of-N would get close to 'right if any sample is right'. But the hardest questions would stay stuck: a perfect checker still can't pick a right answer the model never produces, so a bigger model would still win there.

apply.task: Use the paper's FLOPs formula, inference multiplier = M + 3(M − 1)/R, to work out how much test-time compute a small model may spend to match a 14× bigger one at R = 1 and at R = 100. Then say which regime favours test-time compute.
apply.done: You get 14 + 39 = 53× at R = 1 and 14 + 0.39 = 14.39× at R = 100. Light usage (small R) favours test-time compute.
apply.hint: With M = 14, 3(M − 1) = 39, so the multiplier is 14 + 39/R.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong before reading: how much 16 tries help a question the model gets right 0% of the time?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why revisions suit easy questions, or why heavy usage favours a bigger model?
